insights: High cohesion (1) — files are tightly interconnected
Perfect cohesion (1.0) and zero coupling confirm this zone is correctly scoped as a pure bootstrapping layer with no upstream dependencies leaking in.

Zero coupling is framework-mediated: routes.ts references route files as string literals, so the shell never imports game-ui-routes modules — this is a React Router v7 idiom, not discipline that needs manual maintenance.
Keep this zone minimal — any logic creeping into root.tsx signals it belongs in the engine or components zones.
Cohesion of 1.0 with 3 files is ideal for an entry-point zone; no refactoring needed here.
Zero outbound coupling means the shell never short-circuits zone architecture by importing engine internals directly.
String-literal route registration in routes.ts delivers true zero-coupling without any dependency-inversion machinery — this pattern should be preserved as routes grow.

home.tsx has no zone-documentation comment, unlike play.tsx ('gameplay-ui zone') and worlds.tsx which carry explicit zone headers — the landing route is the only route with no declared architectural context.

home.tsx is the only route file without a zone-documentation comment. play.tsx and worlds.tsx both open with a zone header that states their coupling budget and supplier zones. Adding an equivalent comment to home.tsx (even a minimal one noting it has zero hook/component imports) keeps the documentation pattern consistent and makes the route's intentional simplicity explicit rather than ambiguous.

deploy.sh has zero coupling to the rest of the codebase, which is correct; avoid importing or sourcing application config files from it to preserve this isolation

zones.name: Game Engine
zones.description: The core game loop, state-management hooks, biome theming, canvas rendering, and board utilities that implement all gameplay logic, exposed through dual barrels for types and runtime behavior.
insights: High cohesion (0.92) — files are tightly interconnected
Contains 52% of project files (32/61) — may be too broad, consider splitting
Exceptional cohesion (0.93) across 31 files confirms the import-graph community detection found a real semantic cluster — the engine is the well-bounded architectural core of the application.

The hooks/engine barrel split (hooks=runtime behavior, engine=types-only) is a clean interface-segregation pattern, but it is undocumented and relies entirely on consumer discipline; without barrel-level JSDoc or enforced export separation, this contract will erode as the codebase grows.

app/hooks/ is a separate enforcement layer in check-layers.sh but is folded into game-engine at the zone level — a direct app/engine/* → app/hooks/* import violates the 4-layer DAG but is undetectable by zone-boundaries.test.ts, creating a shared blind spot between the two enforcement systems.
Low coupling (0.07) confirms engine logic is self-sufficient with no hidden dependencies on route or shell layers.

Pure game logic (app/engine/) and React integration layer (app/hooks/) are merged into one zone with no sub-boundary — the informal engine/hooks separation is only enforced by check-layers.sh directory patterns, not by zone-boundaries.test.ts.

`__standaloneInstanceCount` in useSave.ts is a mutable `let` export marked `@internal` by doc comment only — move it to a test-utility module or replace with a read-only getter to prevent test code from mutating production state.

The hooks barrel (app/hooks/index.ts) is explicitly documented with a machine-readable contract comment: it is the ONLY layer that bridges the pure engine into React's stateful world, and it re-exports SaveData type from services so that routes can access domain types without a direct services import — this formalizes the hooks barrel as an anti-corruption layer, not just a convenience re-export.

The components barrel (app/components/index.ts) intentionally withholds board-utils, canvas-drawing, and inventory-shared from its public exports, enforcing encapsulation of internal rendering utilities at the barrel level rather than the file-system level — callers outside the zone have no structural path to these files through the barrel.

The engine barrel (app/engine/index.ts) carries an explicit machine-readable contract comment prohibiting React hooks, stateful singletons, and side-effect-bearing exports — this makes the pure/stateful split between ~/engine and ~/hooks self-documenting and partially refutes the existing insight that the split 'relies entirely on consumer discipline'.

Hooks barrel re-exports SaveData type from services, acting as a deliberate type facade: routes access persistence domain types through ~/hooks without ever importing ~/services directly — this is a clean anti-corruption layer pattern that should be preserved as the services surface grows.

Components barrel suppresses board-utils, canvas-drawing, and inventory-shared from its public API — internal rendering details are barrel-private, but there is no ESLint rule preventing a route from importing these files directly via relative path, leaving encapsulation enforced only by convention.

useGameSession.ts exports resolveCellClickAction and guardNextLevel as plain public exports with no @internal marker or JSDoc annotation — these test helpers are promoted into the hooks barrel's public surface area, creating ambiguity about whether they are part of the stable API or implementation details for tests only.

useGameSession.ts:4 imports SaveData from '~/services/persistence' directly rather than from the '~/services' barrel — this bypasses the services barrel discipline that every other cross-zone import in the project observes, and creates an inconsistency that is not caught by the current ESLint no-restricted-paths rules because the hooks→services edge is permitted at any depth.

useSave.ts runtime warning (standaloneInstanceCount > 1) is the sole enforcement mechanism for the SaveProvider composition requirement — there is no static or compile-time check preventing a route that adds a second save-consuming hook from silently diverging save state in production builds where the warning is stripped.

useGameSession.ts imports SaveData from '~/services/persistence' (deep import) instead of '~/services' (barrel), violating barrel discipline that is consistently observed by every other cross-zone import in the codebase. ESLint permits the edge so this is currently invisible to enforcement.

resolveCellClickAction and guardNextLevel in useGameSession.ts are exported without @internal markers and are therefore visible as part of the hooks zone's public API surface. They are re-exported through the hooks barrel by virtue of the export being public, creating undocumented API surface that consumers could depend on.

useGameState.ts exports both the hook function and UseGameStateReturn interface as fully public symbols, but the hooks barrel intentionally omits both from its public API — there is no comment in either useGameState.ts or hooks/index.ts documenting this barrel-private intent, leaving the exported public interface misleading to any developer reading the file in isolation.

useLevelById.ts is the only hook in the zone without a UseXReturn interface: every other hook (useGameState, useGameSession, useWorldSession, useRainbowEasterEgg, useSave) exports a formal UseXReturn contract. useLevelById returns LevelData | undefined inline; the barrel cannot export a corresponding type export, creating a visible asymmetry in the barrel's export list (line 33 has no companion export type line).

The SAVE_CONSUMING_HOOKS exhaustiveness guard in useSave.test.ts (lines 91–108) detects consumers by scanning for useSave() call-site text and capturing the hook name via regex /export function (use\w+)/. This fails silently for hooks exported as arrow functions (export const useX = ...) — if a future hook adopts arrow-function style, it would call useSave() without being detected, leaving SAVE_CONSUMING_HOOKS stale with no test failure.

useGameState.ts is barrel-private (omitted from hooks/index.ts) but its public exports — useGameState and UseGameStateReturn — carry no documentation of this intent. Add a comment to both useGameState.ts and hooks/index.ts explaining that useGameState is an intra-zone implementation detail composed by useGameSession, not a public hook. This closes the gap between the file-level public surface and the barrel-level encapsulation.

useLevelById.ts is the only hook without a UseXReturn interface, breaking the established return-type contract pattern used by every other hook in the zone. Adding `export interface UseLevelByIdReturn { level: LevelData | undefined }` would allow the barrel to export the type alongside the hook (matching the export pattern on all other lines in hooks/index.ts) and make the return contract explicit.

The SAVE_CONSUMING_HOOKS exhaustiveness guard (useSave.test.ts lines 91–108) uses a regex that only detects hooks declared as `export function useX`. A hook declared as `export const useX = () => {}` would call useSave() without triggering detection, silently leaving the guard list stale. Broaden the regex to cover both declaration forms, or replace the text-scan with an import-based approach.

check-layers.sh (scripts zone) and zone-boundaries.test.ts (project-infrastructure) enforce architectural rules at different abstraction levels; updating one without the other can produce contradictory signals.

react-router.config.ts is the authoritative route registry but has no corresponding zone-boundaries assertion — a route registered at an unconventional path would bypass both ESLint layer rules and zone enforcement silently.

Components barrel suppresses board-utils, canvas-drawing, and inventory-shared from its public API — internal rendering details are barrel-private, but there is no ESLint rule preventing a route from importing these files directly via relative path, leaving encapsulation enforced only by convention.

Hooks barrel re-exports SaveData type from services, acting as a deliberate type facade: routes access persistence domain types through ~/hooks without ever importing ~/services directly — this is a clean anti-corruption layer pattern that should be preserved as the services surface grows.

Triple enforcement consistency meta-test (ESLint + check-layers.sh + zone-boundaries expectations) is a proactive drift-prevention mechanism; it is only as strong as its own coverage — verify that the meta-test itself is included in CI and cannot be skipped independently of the layer tests.

RainbowArc.tsx imports geometry constants via ~/geometry/rainbow-arc (direct) while ~/engine already re-exports those same symbols — replace the direct geometry import with ~/engine to eliminate the undocumented direct game-ui-routes→geometry-primitives coupling edge and restore barrel contract integrity.

geometry-primitives currently has two consumers in the import graph: game-engine (via engine barrel, correct) and game-ui-routes (via RainbowArc direct import, incorrect) — eliminating the direct RainbowArc import would restore geometry-primitives to a single-consumer zone, making the engine barrel the sole and verifiable gate into this zone.

resolveCellClickAction and guardNextLevel in useGameSession.ts are exported without @internal markers and are therefore visible as part of the hooks zone's public API surface. useGameSession.ts imports SaveData from '~/services/persistence' (deep import) instead of '~/services' (barrel), violating barrel discipline that is consistently observed by every other cross-zone import in the codebase. ESLint permits the edge so this is currently invisible to enforcement.

The services zone is the only non-leaf application zone without an inbound barrel-enforcement ESLint rule. Engine, hooks, and components all have rules that block deep imports from outside the zone; services has no equivalent rule. The asymmetry means a developer can add a new internal services file and it is immediately accessible to hooks via direct path with no lint warning.

useSave.ts, useGameSession.ts, and useWorldSession.ts all import from ~/services/persistence directly rather than ~/services barrel. The services barrel is bypassed by every hook that consumes it, making it a re-export facade that provides no actual access control. This is inconsistent with the barrel-as-contract pattern enforced for engine, hooks, and components zones.

The SAVE_CONSUMING_HOOKS exhaustiveness guard (useSave.test.ts lines 91–108) uses a regex that only detects hooks declared as `export function useX`. A hook declared as `export const useX = () => {}` would call useSave() without triggering detection, silently leaving the guard list stale. Broaden the regex to cover both declaration forms, or replace the text-scan with an import-based approach.

useGameState.ts is barrel-private (omitted from hooks/index.ts) but its public exports — useGameState and UseGameStateReturn — carry no documentation of this intent. useLevelById.ts is the only hook without a UseXReturn interface, breaking the established return-type contract pattern used by every other hook in the zone. Adding `export interface UseLevelByIdReturn { level: LevelData | undefined }` would allow the barrel to export the type alongside the hook (matching the export pattern on all other lines in hooks/index.ts) and make the return contract explicit.

The SaveProvider architectural invariant is currently enforced by two mechanisms at different abstraction levels: a runtime dev-mode warning in useSave.ts and a static fs-scan test in useSave.test.ts. The static test cross-zone reads route files from a hooks-zone test, which is the only instance of this pattern in the project. Consolidating this assertion into zone-boundaries.test.ts (which already does cross-zone static analysis) would unify the two enforcement levels and eliminate the hidden cross-zone read dependency.
